Overview: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the most common form of urinary tract infection in the United States. UTIs are more common in women than in men due to anatomical differences such as a shorter urethra and its proximity to the anus, which facilitates bacterial entry into the urinary tract. UTIs are the most common cause of serious bacterial illness, with up to 8% of girls and 2% of boys developing at least one UTI by age seven.

Causes: Causes of UTIs The overwhelming majority of UTIs, approximately 80% or more, are caused by *Escherichia coli* (UPEC ). Fungal pathogens, particularly *Candida* species, can also cause UTIs, especially in immunocompromised individuals . Several risk factors contribute to the development of UTIs
Treatment: Antimicrobial stewardship Antimicrobial stewardship is crucial to combat the rising issue of antimicrobial resistance. Fluoroquinolones are generally reserved for complicated cases or when other options are not suitable, given concerns about potential adverse effects. Severe cases may necessitate initial intravenous (IV) antimicrobials (e.g., ceftriaxone 500 mg twice daily for 7 days) followed by a step-down to oral antibiotics (e.g., cefpodoxime 100 mg twice daily for 10–14 days).
